content: Congenital choanal atresia is a rare condition in which the posterior part of the nasal cavity is either partially or completely blocked, occurring on one or both sides. This condition is observed in approximately 1 in 5,000 to 1 in 8,000 live births and is twice as common in females compared to males. Surgical intervention is the primary treatment, with the goals of achieving adequate and lasting nasal airway patency, minimizing the risk of restenosis, avoiding damage to developing structures, reducing the duration of surgery and hospitalization, and lowering the associated morbidity and mortality. The objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness and safety of various surgical techniques used to treat congenital choanal atresia in patients with either unilateral or bilateral forms of the condition. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Ear, Nose and Throat Disorders Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, PubMed, EMBASE, CINAHL, Web of Science, BIOSIS Previews, Cambridge Scientific Abstracts, ISRCTN, and other sources. The search was completed on January 31, 2011. The inclusion criteria for this review were parallel randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials that evaluated surgical approaches for congenital choanal atresia, regardless of the patient’s age or gender. The primary outcomes of interest were the restoration or maintenance of normal respiratory function (either self-reported or objectively measured) and the occurrence of restenosis. Studies involving reoperations or non-congenital forms of atresia, such as those caused by trauma or medical interventions, were excluded. Three independent reviewers assessed the titles and abstracts of the identified studies to determine their relevance. For dichotomous outcomes, risk ratios (relative risks) with 95% confidence intervals were planned for calculation, while mean differences with 95% confidence intervals were planned for continuous outcomes. A random-effects model was intended for use due to the anticipated clinical and methodological variability among studies. Despite an extensive search that yielded 120 reports, no randomized controlled trials were identified. Of these, 46 primary studies initially appeared to meet the inclusion criteria, as they evaluated surgical techniques for choanal atresia. However, all of these studies were excluded during the final selection process because their designs did not align with the inclusion criteria. In conclusion, there is currently no high-quality evidence from randomized controlled trials to support or refute the benefits and risks of specific surgical techniques for the treatment of congenital choanal atresia. The authors emphasize the need for collaborative efforts among specialists to conduct multicenter randomized controlled trials to rigorously evaluate the safety and efficacy of different surgical approaches for this condition.
